description: Width tiers for Languages — F-10 sequence, Year 3-4 band. All standards are capability descriptors. C strand standards use task_contexts as the primary width axis. U strand standards use phenomena_contexts (Systems of language and Language and culture). At this band students move from responding to modelled language to initiating exchanges, planning with others, and developing explicit comprehension and cultural meaning strategies.
subject: Languages

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single task context or phenomenon that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For C strand: minimum is the narrowest communicative context in which the described initiation, participation or creation is genuine — not only responding to direct teacher prompts. For U strand: minimum is engagement with the described language feature or cultural connection in at least one context with evidence of understanding.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. For C strand: a range of task types and communicative contexts that reflect the descriptor's interactional, mediating or creative intent. For U strand: the range of language features, metalanguage and cultural connections described in the elaborations.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new communicative contexts, cultural communities, comparison languages or task types. Width adds breadth of context — not difficulty of the same task. For U strand: additional language features, text types for comparison, or cultural contexts that deepen language understanding.
width_notes.elaborations: Target language (F-10 sequence) elaborations were used as the primary source. All target-language-specific vocabulary and grammar examples have been genericised. Elaborations are preserved verbatim in each standard entry as source record.

AC9LS4C01.minimum_width: Initiate at least one exchange using an appropriate greeting or opening question without teacher prompting; respond to at least three different personal questions using modelled sentence structures.
AC9LS4C01.typical_width: Initiate and respond to exchanges about self, family, friends, interests, school and home life across a range of familiar contexts. Use formal and informal greetings appropriately. Use a range of interrogatives to obtain information. Describe routines, preferences and locations. Make and respond to requests for clarification, repetition and help.
wider: Conduct a short unrehearsed exchange with a partner — initiating, sustaining and closing without teacher scripting — using at least four different question types
Exchange information about routines across different time frames and explain the pattern of a typical week in the target language
Explain to a partner the strategies available when communication breaks down in the target language — listing at least three metacommunicative expressions
elaborations: using formal and informal greetings in a variety of contexts
exchanging information about family, friends or interests using simple descriptive statements and conjunctions
using question-answer patterns to share information about school and home life
responding to simple questions about the class environment or daily routine
explaining routines and favourite activities using expressions related to time and days of the week
using a range of interrogatives to obtain further details
describing features, characteristics and locations of particular things or places
making and responding to requests such as asking for items, requesting help, clarification, rephrasing or repetition

AC9LS4C02.minimum_width: Use at least two turn-taking or task allocation expressions in a collaborative activity; follow or produce at least one sequenced procedure using step language.
AC9LS4C02.typical_width: Participate in planning activities with others — using turn-taking, complimenting and task allocation language, sequencing procedures step by step, creating invitations and collaborative outputs for events, and making group decisions. Produce shared outputs across varied task types (event plans, menus, scripts, picture books).
wider: Lead a group through a procedure in the target language — calling each step, checking completion and handing over to the next person
Create an invitation for a real class event in the target language — making deliberate decisions about content, vocabulary and audience
Plan and present a collaborative project for a real audience (buddy class, school event) using task allocation and sequencing language throughout
elaborations: negotiating and confirming turn-taking and complimenting friends
making matching-pair games with target language and English word cards
creating simple action songs and games that include alternating repetitive phrases
following procedures such as a simple recipe, craft making or science experiment, and repeating language of sequencing and instructions
working together to write, rehearse and present a simple plan or script for a special event
planning a puppet show, canteen menu or picture book for a buddy class, and collaborating on content, vocabulary and design
working with visual, print and digital modes to create invitations for a party, performance or class event
participating in organising a shared lunch or class party, discussing who will bring what and run activities

AC9LS4C03.minimum_width: Locate specific information from at least two different text types without direct teacher prompting for each item; organise located information into an appropriate graphic format.
AC9LS4C03.typical_width: Locate and respond to key information across a range of familiar spoken, written and multimodal texts — stories, weather reports, menus, advertisements, surveys. Categorise information using tables, graphs and diagrams. Survey classmates and represent data visually. Express personal reactions to text content. Adapt familiar texts for new purposes.
wider: Research a topic using two or more sources and compare what each includes — identify what the different sources add to understanding
Produce a data representation from peer survey data — select the most appropriate format and explain what the data shows
Create an adaptation of a familiar text that changes at least the setting and one key event — explaining the choices made
elaborations: questioning or surveying classmates about likes and dislikes and representing data in various formats
researching aspects of target language communities and presenting information in new ways
comparing information about activities and practices in a target language community and Australia
learning that First Nations Australian languages change according to connections and relationships between people, and giving examples of how this occurs in the target language
listening to, reading or viewing a range of texts and responding to questions about characters, ideas and events
expressing personal reactions to characters or events in texts using props such as puppets or masks
using a range of techniques to act out or animate the key physical and character traits of well-known characters
creating adaptations of well-known stories using familiar phrases
categorising information from a range of texts using tables, graphs and diagrams
listening to factual reports and creating an invitation for a friend, incorporating elements from the text

AC9LS4C04.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words in a text; use appropriate formality in at least two different social contexts.
AC9LS4C04.typical_width: Develop and apply strategies to comprehend unfamiliar target language — using context, cognates, surrounding words, dictionaries and English literacy knowledge. Adjust language for formality and cultural meaning across familiar contexts. Identify culturally specific expressions that require explanation to non-target-language speakers. Compare target language and English expressions for cultural nuance.
wider: Apply multiple strategies to the same unfamiliar word and compare which gives the most accurate result — articulate a personal strategy priority for target language comprehension
Identify a culturally specific target language expression and explain what cultural knowledge is needed to understand it — produce an explanation for a non-target-language speaker
Compare the level of formality in two versions of the same social situation — explain every language difference and the cultural reason for it
elaborations: comparing target language expressions used in routine social interactions with equivalent English expressions, identifying similarities, differences and cultural references
matching signs from target language communities with equivalents found in Australia
applying knowledge of the alphabet to use a picture or online dictionary
knowing when to apply varying levels of formality and showing respect depending on occasion, context and relationship
explaining interactions when using the target language that look or feel different from interactions in their own language
identifying words, expressions or conventions in the target language that would need explaining to a non-target-language speaker
considering context and audience, noticing surrounding words to infer or guess the meaning of new words
applying English literacy skills to support understanding of new words in target language texts
commenting on culturally specific elements of stories or songs

AC9LS4C05.minimum_width: Create an informative text with at least five target language elements appropriate to the topic; present the text to an audience using appropriate spoken support.
AC9LS4C05.typical_width: Create and present informative and imaginative texts across a range of formats — reports, profiles, displays, puppet shows, adapted stories, alternative songs, bilingual texts, greeting cards, map descriptions — using formulaic expressions, simple phrases and modelled textual conventions. Create for real audiences where possible.
wider: Create an informative text on a target language community topic that goes beyond copying facts — selecting the most interesting information and explaining why it was chosen
Perform an imaginative text for a genuine audience (buddy class, assembly) — adapting the presentation for the audience's level of target language knowledge
Create a bilingual text for a specified audience — making deliberate decisions about which language to use for which part and explaining the choice
elaborations: creating a class report or visual/digital display related to topics studied in the target language and/or other learning areas
planning and presenting information on cultural events of interest to peers
using innovative ways to create a self-profile or self-introduction
creating simple descriptions in the target language and matching them to First Nations Country/Place locations
recreating familiar stories or fables to share with younger learners
writing the first part of a short imaginative text and exchanging with others to complete
singing or reciting alternative versions of familiar songs or rhymes
creating simple bilingual texts
making a sculpture and annotating it in the target language
researching a target language community and writing a packing list appropriate for its conditions

AC9LS4U01.minimum_width: Use sound knowledge to predict the spelling of at least two unfamiliar target language words based on known patterns; identify at least one consonant blend or digraph in context.
AC9LS4U01.typical_width: Recognise and use modelled combinations of sounds, pronunciation and intonation patterns — applying spelling prediction from sound patterns, recognising consonant blends, using accent marks correctly, distinguishing intonation across sentence types (statements, questions, commands, exclamations), and using onomatopoeia in context.
wider: Explain a target language spelling rule using examples — demonstrating metalinguistic understanding of the pattern
Demonstrate how changing only intonation changes the meaning of the same sentence — produce at least three intonation variants and explain the communicative difference
Compare target language and English onomatopoeia for the same sounds — identify where conventions are similar and where they differ
elaborations: applying rules of silent letters and recognising that loan words may follow similar patterns
recognising and using different intonation for statements, commands, exclamations and questions
using knowledge of familiar sounds and patterns to spell new words
playing games with more difficult sounds
exploring the function of accents in relation to stress and pronunciation
understanding that some letters blend to make single sounds
using onomatopoeia during group reading and spoken text, for animal sounds, actions and reactions

AC9LS4U02.minimum_width: Use correct plural gender/class agreement in at least two noun phrases; use at least three different possessive adjectives correctly in context.
AC9LS4U02.typical_width: Recognise and use target language grammatical structures and syntax — including personal pronouns, plural and gender/class agreement, possessive adjectives in singular and plural forms, common verbs in familiar forms, prepositions for location, adverbs for time, conjunctions to link ideas, question words, imperatives, and numbers for time, dates and age.
wider: Write connected sentences using a different conjunction in each — demonstrating range beyond the most basic connectors
Produce a paragraph using both forms of 'to be' (or equivalent grammatical distinction) correctly — and explain (in English) why each was used
Find target language nouns that do not follow the regular gender/class pattern — explain how their class is signalled in context
elaborations: using personal pronouns
exploring the use and omission of subject pronouns by looking at verb endings and conjugations
identifying the use of familiar singular, plural and gender forms in simple sentences
using some possessive adjectives in familiar singular and plural forms
identifying nouns that do not follow the regular gender/class ending pattern
using numbers in context to indicate quantity, tell the time, dates and ages
applying modelled punctuation and capitalisation rules when writing
specifying location or direction using prepositions
using and responding to imperatives
using question words in modelled structures
using a range of adjectives to describe appearance, feelings and personality
using common verbs in familiar contexts
using adverbs to locate events in time
linking simple ideas using conjunctions

AC9LS4U03.minimum_width: Use at least four metalanguage terms correctly to describe target language grammatical features; identify at least two target language-English cognate pairs using a systematic pattern.
AC9LS4U03.typical_width: Recognise familiar target language language features and compare with English — using grammatical metalanguage in both languages, recognising systematic cognate suffix patterns, comparing features of similar text types across the two languages, and applying English punctuation knowledge to target language texts.
wider: Apply a systematic cognate pattern to predict the English equivalent of unfamiliar target language words — test predictions and identify exceptions
Produce a bilingual grammar glossary for at least six terms — defining each in both languages with an example sentence
Find an authentic target language text of a familiar type and compare it line by line with an English equivalent — annotate every difference noticed
elaborations: building metalanguage to talk about grammar and vocabulary, and comparing with equivalent terms in English
recognising similarities and differences between spoken and written forms of different types of texts in both languages
comparing features of similar texts in the target language and English
recognising language of familiarity and how the language of texts such as invitations may vary depending on the relationship
using English punctuation knowledge to apply to target language texts and to compare punctuation use
beginning to recognise target language cognate patterns shared with English

AC9LS4U04.minimum_width: Use at least two conceptual terms (identity, behaviour, celebration, belief) when discussing a target language language-culture connection; explain at least one connection between a language feature and a cultural practice.
AC9LS4U04.typical_width: Identify connections between the target language and cultural practices — using conceptual vocabulary (identity, behaviour, celebrations, beliefs), exploring how language features carry cultural meaning (e.g. naming conventions, diminutives, forms of address), and reflecting on cross-cultural comparisons. Engage with First Nations Australian cultural expressions and connect with target language cultural parallels.
wider: Research a target language cultural practice and explain the language associated with it — using at least three conceptual terms to frame the explanation
Explore representations used in cultural expressions of First Nations Australians and find parallel patterns in target language community cultural expressions
Reflect on a moment where target language cultural conventions felt different from their own — describe the language, the behaviour and their reaction, and explain what the difference reveals
elaborations: using terms such as identity, behaviour, celebrations and beliefs to talk about language and culture
expressing reactions to ways of communicating or behaving in the target language that feel familiar or different
reflecting on how they communicate with family, friends and unfamiliar adults, noticing differences in language use
exploring representations of information used in cultural expressions of First Nations Australians and making connections with those of target language culture
understanding that language carries information about the people who use it and that common expressions often reflect cultural values
finding examples of words and expressions introduced into the target language in recent times, reflecting changes in cultural experience
